views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: China should maintain its retaliatory posture (sorghum investigation) as a signal of willingness to fight, while quietly pursuing back-channel negotiations with the US before the Section 301 findings land. Do not escalate further — soybean tariffs would hurt Chinese consumers more than they punish the US. Instead, offer selective market-access openings and IP reform language that buys time without surrendering core strategic objectives under Made in China 2025.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat_score of +0.35 reflects that the dispute is serious but not yet existential for China. The Section 301 investigation (initiated Aug 2017, timeline entry) targets China's forced technology transfer regime, cyber-enabled IP theft, and state-directed acquisition of US tech firms — all pillars of China's industrial upgrading strategy. USTR findings are imminent and will likely recommend tariffs on $50-60B of Chinese imports in advanced-technology sectors. However, China's economy posted 6.9% GDP growth in 2017 (country_health / web_search), reserves stand at ~$3T, and the direct macro impact so far is limited to solar/washer tariffs (Jan 2018 timeline entry) — a relatively contained first salvo. The threat is elevated but manageable at this stage.

The action_score of -0.15 (mildly escalatory, within negotiate band) reflects the need to signal resolve without provoking a cascade. China's sorghum anti-dumping investigation (Feb 2018, web_search) has already demonstrated willingness to retaliate, targeting Trump's agricultural voter base. This is smart asymmetric signaling — the $1B sorghum trade is small enough not to trigger catastrophic escalation but politically potent enough to register. However, further escalation (soybeans, Treasuries) would be self-defeating: China imported $12.4B of US soybeans in 2016, and restricting supply would raise domestic food prices and hog-feed costs (web_search: farmpolicynews). Selling US Treasuries would weaken the dollar and hurt China's own export competitiveness (NYT, Jan 2018). The US economy is strong (industrial production rising, consumer sentiment at 99.7), giving Washington little domestic pressure to back down. China's leverage is real but asymmetric — it can inflict pain but cannot win an escalating trade war. Negotiation, not escalation, preserves optionality.
key_factors: Section 301 investigation findings imminent — likely to target $50-60B of Chinese tech exports
China's sorghum retaliation signals resolve but is proportionate
US economy strong (IP rising, sentiment high) — limited domestic pressure on Trump to de-escalate
China GDP 6.9%, reserves ~$3T — buffers exist but export model is vulnerable
Soybean/Treasury retaliation would be self-defeating for China
Made in China 2025 industrial strategy directly in US crosshairs

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump signs memorandum directing USTR to investigate China's IP and technology-transfer practices under Section 301.
Trump approves Section 201 safeguard tariffs on solar panels and washing machines (China among suppliers hit).
US Industrial Production rising steadily to 101.71 (Feb 2018)
China has opened an anti-dumping and anti-subsidy investigation into sorghum imports from the United States, less than a fortnight after US imposed tariffs on solar panels and washing machines.
China is studying the potential impact of trade measures imposed on soybeans imported from the U.S., valued last year at $13.9 billion.

While Chinese officials have many options with which to retaliate against potential United States tariffs, they have few good ones. Beijing would weaken the dollar if it sold Treasuries, which might in turn reduce the competitiveness of Chinese goods abroad.
